summary.case_overview: This judgment arises from Writ Petition (Civil) No. 494 of 2012, Justice K. S. Puttaswamy (Retd.) and Anr. v. Union of India and Ors., decided on August 24, 2017, by a 9-judge Constitution Bench of the Supreme Court of India [Page 1]. The reference was triggered by a constitutional challenge to the Government of India's Aadhaar card scheme, under which demographic and biometric data of residents were collected and compiled [Page 15]. The primary legal question before the 9-judge Bench was whether the right to privacy is a fundamental right under the Constitution of India, in light of earlier larger-bench decisions in M. P. Sharma (8 judges) and Kharak Singh (6 judges) which had held that privacy was not a guaranteed fundamental right [Page 1] [Page 78]. The Supreme Court unanimously held that the right to privacy is a fundamental right protected as an intrinsic part of the right to life and personal liberty under Article 21 and as part of the freedoms guaranteed by Part III of the Constitution [Page 1] [Page 15] [Page 431].
summary.facts_of_case: The Government of India propounded the Aadhaar card scheme, under which demographic and biometric data of Indian residents were collected and compiled to be used for various official purposes [Page 15]. A batch of petitions was filed challenging the scheme on the ground that the compulsory collection and compilation of such personal data violated the fundamental right to privacy [Page 15]. During the hearings, the Union of India and state respondents relied upon the 8-judge Bench judgment in M. P. Sharma (1954) and the 6-judge Bench judgment in Kharak Singh (1962) to contend that the Indian Constitution does not recognize or guarantee a fundamental right to privacy [Page 1] [Page 78]. Noting an apparent contradiction between these larger-bench decisions and several subsequent smaller-bench judgments that had recognized privacy as a fundamental right, a three-judge Bench referred the matter to a larger Bench [Page 78]. On July 18, 2017, a Constitution Bench presided over by the Chief Justice referred the core question regarding the existence and status of the fundamental right to privacy to a 9-judge Bench [Page 78].
summary.legal_issues: The major constitutional issues considered by the 9-judge Bench were: (1) Whether the decision in M. P. Sharma v. Satish Chandra correctly held that the right to privacy is not protected by the Indian Constitution [Page 1] [Page 78] [Page 430]; (2) Whether the decision in Kharak Singh v. State of U.P., to the extent that it held that the right to privacy is not protected under the Constitution, reflects the correct legal position [Page 1] [Page 78] [Page 430]; (3) Whether the right to privacy is an inalienable fundamental right protected under Article 21 and Part III of the Constitution of India, and if so, what are its facets, scope, and permissible restrictions [Page 1] [Page 3] [Page 15] [Page 277].
summary.important_arguments_or_content: The petitioners argued that the collection of biometric and demographic data under the Aadhaar scheme infringes upon an individual's personal autonomy and privacy [Page 15] [Page 428]. They submitted that modern technology allows invasive intrusion into an individual's life and personal space without physical entry, making privacy a vital constitutional firewall against State and non-State overreach [Page 10] [Page 409] [Page 428]. The Union of India and respondents submitted that there is no fundamental right to privacy explicitly mentioned in the Constitution [Page 78]. They argued that reading privacy into Part III would require a formal constitutional amendment rather than judicial interpretation, relying heavily on M. P. Sharma and Kharak Singh [Page 2] [Page 19] [Page 78]. The respondents further contended that privacy interests are adequately addressed by ordinary statutory law and policy rather than constitutional guarantees [Page 13] [Page 427].
summary.court_reasoning: The Court observed that M. P. Sharma was primarily concerned with search and seizure under Article 20(3) in the absence of a provision like the US Fourth Amendment, and did not rule out privacy as an aspect of Article 21 or other Part III freedoms [Page 1] [Page 5] [Page 34] [Page 354]. Regarding Kharak Singh, the Court noted an internal inconsistency in the majority opinion: while it rightly struck down night-time domiciliary visits for violating ordered liberty, its second conclusion that privacy is not guaranteed was logically unsound and incorrect [Page 1] [Page 2] [Page 5] [Page 6] [Page 122]. The Court held that fundamental rights are natural, inalienable human rights that inhere in every individual by birth and pre-exist the Constitution; they are not bounties granted by the State [Page 4] [Page 8] [Page 9] [Page 14] [Page 15] [Page 166]. Dignity and liberty, emphasized in the Preamble, form the core of Article 21 and Part III, and privacy is an essential condition for exercising personal liberty and leading a life with dignity [Page 2] [Page 7] [Page 9] [Page 18] [Page 398]. The Court ruled that privacy has multiple facets—including spatial, decisional, and informational privacy—and protects personal choices regarding family, marriage, procreation, and sexual orientation [Page 3] [Page 10] [Page 14] [Page 233] [Page 419] [Page 428]. The Court also highlighted that privacy is not an absolute right; any State restriction on privacy must pass the threefold test of: (i) legality (existence of a valid law), (ii) legitimate State interest (need), and (iii) proportionality (rational nexus between object and means) [Page 3] [Page 277] [Page 424]. Additionally, the majority opinion in ADM Jabalpur v. Shivkant Shukla was expressly overruled as a serious flaw in constitutional jurisprudence [Page 20] [Page 166] [Page 430].
summary.decision_or_conclusion: The 9-judge Bench unanimously disposed of the reference in the following terms: (i) The decision in M. P. Sharma holding that the right to privacy is not protected by the Constitution is overruled [Page 1] [Page 15] [Page 430]; (ii) The decision in Kharak Singh to the extent that it holds that the right to privacy is not protected by the Constitution is overruled [Page 1] [Page 15] [Page 430] [Page 431]; (iii) The right to privacy is protected as an intrinsic part of the right to life and personal liberty under Article 21 and as part of the freedoms guaranteed by Part III of the Constitution [Page 1] [Page 15] [Page 431]; (iv) Decisions subsequent to Kharak Singh enunciating that privacy is a fundamental right lay down the correct legal position [Page 15] [Page 431]. The batch of writ petitions was ordered to be sent back to a three-judge Bench for final adjudication on merits in light of this judgment [Page 5].

summary.simplified_explanation: In this landmark ruling, a 9-judge Bench of the Supreme Court of India decided whether citizens have a fundamental right to privacy [Page 1] [Page 78]. The Court unanimously held that privacy is an inherent human right that every person is born with [Page 1] [Page 9] [Page 15]. It is protected under Article 21 of the Constitution as part of the right to life and personal liberty [Page 1] [Page 2] [Page 15]. This decision officially overturned older court rulings from 1954 and 1962 which had claimed privacy was not guaranteed by the Constitution [Page 1] [Page 15] [Page 430]. The Court clarified that privacy protects a person's body, personal space, private choices (like marriage and lifestyle), and personal digital data [Page 3] [Page 10] [Page 233] [Page 419]. However, privacy is not absolute; the government can restrict it only if there is a clear law, a valid public purpose, and the restriction is proportionate to the goal [Page 3] [Page 277] [Page 424].
